section_summary: This section traces U.S. diplomatic and military reporting on Japanese activity in Costa Rica from 1932 to 1939. Initial inquiries found no evidence of Japanese coastal surveying, but later reports treated fishing ventures, cotton experiments, commercial propaganda, immigration and reconnaissance around Puntarenas, Guanacaste and Golfo Dulce as possible covers for espionage or preparations affecting the Panama Canal. The section also contains correspondence about the financially troubled Pacific Refrigeration Company, Japanese efforts to cultivate Costa Rican political goodwill, and Colonel Gerard F. Montúfar's unsolicited warning about Japanese influence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 842: Topographical Survey by Japanese
subfiles.from: Charles C. Eberhardt, American Minister at San José
subfiles.about: Reports preliminary inquiries into alleged Japanese topographical surveying along Costa Rica's coasts.
subfiles.summary: Eberhardt reports that two reliable sources found no evidence of Japanese survey activity on Costa Rica's Pacific coast. He plans a later inquiry at Port Limón and considers it unlikely that such ventures have occurred on either coast, while promising continued surveillance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 891: Topographical Survey by Japanese
subfiles.from: Charles C. Eberhardt, American Minister at San José
subfiles.about: Forwards the Limón vice consul's negative report on Japanese coastal surveying.
subfiles.summary: Eberhardt follows up Despatch No. 842 by enclosing Walter W. Hoffmann's findings. He states that no Japanese were known to have operated in the Limón consular district in connection with presumed surveys.

subfiles.title: Hoffmann report on Japanese activity around Port Limón
subfiles.from: Walter W. Hoffmann, American Vice Consul in Charge at Port Limón
subfiles.about: Reports that no Japanese residents, fishermen or coastal travelers could be found in the Limón district.
subfiles.summary: Hoffmann found no Japanese residents in Port Limón or Limón Province and no evidence of Japanese participation in fishing or coastal shipping. Local crews were chiefly Haitian, Colombian or locally born West Indian, and port records revealed only two Japanese travelers who had passed through briefly in earlier years. He concludes that no Japanese fishing or survey cruises were being conducted there.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese fishing vessels near Puntarenas
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Costa Rica
subfiles.about: Cross-references a telegram concerning Japanese fishing vessels near Puntarenas and Panama Canal defense.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Telegram No. 21 concerning Japanese fishing vessels in Costa Rica. It records the War Department's view that Japanese vessels near Puntarenas would be inimical to the defense of the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: File note on Iwamoto's proposed Puntarenas fishing base
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Costa Rica
subfiles.about: Cross-references negotiations for a Japanese fishing base at Puntarenas.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Despatch No. 813 as concerning Chiyoma Iwamoto's negotiations with the Costa Rican government. Iwamoto represented the Japan Union Fishery Company and sought to establish a fishing base at Puntarenas.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 813: Japanese proposal for a Puntarenas fishing base
subfiles.from: Leo R. Sack, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Reports both changes to an American tuna-plant concession and the arrival of Japanese fishing promoters.
subfiles.summary: Congress approved a modified contract for an American-backed tuna refrigeration plant, but the changes threatened the project's viability. Three Japanese visitors then arrived to propose a fishing base at Puntarenas, including Japan Union Fishery Company representative Chiyoma Iwamoto and his companion Hitsumatsu Fukuno. Sack notes possible links to similar negotiations in El Salvador and promises further investigation.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese pursuit of a fishing concession
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Costa Rica
subfiles.about: Cross-references a communication concerning Japanese interest in a Puntarenas fishing concession.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Despatch No. 829 and an enclosed communication from Alex A. Cohen. It concerns local interest at Puntarenas in a fishing concession sought by two Japanese visitors.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese military activities and proposed cotton colonization
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Panama (Flexer)
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Japanese cotton colonists and Raúl Gurdián's journey through Panama.
subfiles.summary: The note describes proposed cotton cultivation on Costa Rica's Pacific coast by Japanese colonist “experts.” It also records the presence in Panama of former Costa Rican finance minister Raúl Gurdián while he was traveling to Japan.

subfiles.title: File note on Amano Fishing Company negotiations
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Cross-references negotiations for an Amano fish-packing plant at Puntarenas.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Telegram No. 6 as reporting talks between Costa Rican officials and a representative of the Amano Fishing Company of Panama. The proposed venture was a fish-packing plant at Puntarenas.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 6 on Amano Fishing Company
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, San José
subfiles.about: Reports Amano negotiations and orders a discreet inquiry at Puntarenas.
subfiles.summary: Hornibrook reports that a representative of the Japanese Amano Fishing Company, then said to operate in Panama, was negotiating for a large fish-packing plant at Puntarenas. He sent Collins to the port to conduct a discreet survey of Japanese activities.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4,155: Japanese propaganda in Costa Rica
subfiles.from: J. B. Pate, Military Attaché
subfiles.to: U.S. War and State Department channels
subfiles.about: Analyzes a large Japanese commercial advertisement as evidence of an established propaganda agency.
subfiles.summary: The report translates and discusses an advertisement promoting Japanese-Costa Rican trade, coffee purchases and Japanese-sponsored cotton planting. The Military Attaché regards it as confirmation that a permanent Japanese propaganda agency had been established in San José under commercial cover.

subfiles.title: Advertisement of the Official Japanese Federation of Exporters and Importers with Latin America
subfiles.from: Official Japanese Federation of Exporters and Importers with Latin America
subfiles.about: Promotes Japanese trade, credit arrangements and cotton cultivation in Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: The Spanish-language advertisement denies that Costa Rican products bought by Japan would be dumped in other markets and promises payment through the National Bank of Costa Rica. It argues that Japan can provide new markets for coffee and develop resources such as cotton for Costa Rican benefit.

subfiles.title: File note on Wakabayashi as an alleged espionage agent
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report identifying T. Wakabayashi publicly as an espionage agent.
subfiles.summary: The note concerns Japanese activities in Costa Rica and the first public description of T. Wakabayashi as an espionage agent. It points to Despatch No. 129 for the original report.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4,172: Japanese activities in Costa Rica
subfiles.from: J. B. Pate, Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Relays a Costa Rican informant's view that Japanese spending supported either a regional demonstration project or an espionage network.
subfiles.summary: A trusted Costa Rican informant argues that Japanese spending on cotton colonists, officials, advertising and fishing plans was disproportionate to ordinary trade. The informant suggests either a demonstration of Japanese capabilities for Latin America or a coordinated espionage network around the Panama Canal. Wakabayashi is portrayed as a secret-service superior to the Japanese minister, while Hosokawa's Amano fishing negotiations are linked to the broader effort.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4,145: Japanese fishing activities at Puntarenas
subfiles.from: J. B. Pate, Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese fishing vessels at Puntarenas could threaten Panama Canal security.
subfiles.summary: The report says Yoshimoto Hosokawa was negotiating a large Japanese fishing concession at Puntarenas and was associated with five vessels, including the Amano. Pate expects Japanese fishermen displaced by Panama's restrictions to move to Costa Rica and argues that long-range, radio-equipped vessels could support hostile operations near the Panama Canal. He also predicts efforts to gain access to Golfo Dulce, Culebra Bay and Costa Rican radio facilities.

subfiles.title: Translation of La Tribuna article on a Japanese Puntarenas fishery
subfiles.from: La Tribuna, San José
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed large Japanese fishing enterprise at Puntarenas.
subfiles.summary: The article says a Japanese engineer planned to present the government with a contract for a heavily capitalized fishing enterprise. Only a few technicians would be Japanese, while most employees would be Costa Rican, and the newspaper presents the project as a source of prosperity for Puntarenas.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4,192: Japanese reconnaissance and colonization plans
subfiles.from: J. B. Pate, Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Interprets Japanese travel in Guanacaste and Golfo Dulce as strategic reconnaissance.
subfiles.summary: Informants reported four Japanese cotton experts making sketches near Filadelfia in the Tempisque valley and two Japanese led by Yoshimoto Hosokawa visiting Puerto Jiménez to discuss a coconut-oil factory. Pate concludes that Japanese personnel were surveying transportation, communications, potential airfields and Pacific harbors while seeking a permanent colony near deep water. He expects further efforts even if the Puntarenas concession is defeated.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese espionage and declining popularity
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report linking espionage allegations to declining Japanese popularity.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Despatch No. 133 as addressing Japanese espionage in Costa Rica. It records that reporting about espionage had partly caused a substantial recent loss of Japanese popularity.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4,125: Japanese penetration into Costa Rica
subfiles.from: J. B. Pate, Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Compiles Japanese diplomatic, agricultural, propaganda and fishing activities during 1937.
subfiles.summary: Pate provides a chronology covering Minister Saichiro Koshida's visit, cotton concessions, Raúl Gurdián's Japanese-sponsored trip, the arrival of cotton growers from Peru, and Yoshimoto Hosokawa's fishing activities. He alleges that paid publicity, lobbying and political connections were helping Japanese interests resist discriminatory tariffs. Reports of Japanese vessels taking soundings in the Gulf of Nicoya and the unexplained itinerary of the Amano lead him to recommend an undercover agent at Puntarenas.

subfiles.title: File note on a possible Japanese air base in Guanacaste
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Cross-references Colonel Pate's warning about clandestine aircraft assembly in Guanacaste.
subfiles.summary: The note records a conversation in which Colonel Pate suggested that Japanese agents could smuggle airplane parts into Costa Rica. He feared they might assemble aircraft and create an emergency landing field in sparsely settled Guanacaste for operations against the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: File note on refusal of Japanese request for railway data
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Records Costa Rica's refusal to provide railway information to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references Despatch No. 205 on a Japanese request for Costa Rican railway data. Costa Rican officials refused because the information could be employed for purposes other than commerce.

subfiles.title: File note on interdepartmental discussion of Japanese interests
subfiles.from: State Department (Chapin)
subfiles.about: Cross-references a State-War-Navy meeting on Japanese cotton and manganese ventures.
subfiles.summary: The note records a meeting of representatives from the State, War and Navy Departments. Participants considered Japanese interest in cotton plantations and manganese deposits to be a possible blind for military objectives.

subfiles.title: Report on organization of the Amano Fishery Company
subfiles.from: U.S. Military Attaché's office
subfiles.about: Reports the incorporation of an Amano fishing company under Costa Rican law.
subfiles.summary: Citing La Prensa, the report states that the Amano Fishery Company had been organized under Costa Rican law with capital divided into large shares. Its operations were to be based at Puntarenas, and the report characterized the company as another stage in systematic Japanese penetration of Costa Rica.

subfiles.title: Report on an alleged Japanese naval reserve officer near Golfo Dulce
subfiles.from: U.S. Military Attaché's office, citing William H. Hornibrook
subfiles.about: Reports that an alleged Japanese naval reservist took a permanent position at an Osa Peninsula sawmill.
subfiles.summary: Hornibrook's source claimed that a Japanese national formerly serving as chief engineer on a Peruvian ship was also a Japanese naval reserve officer. The man reportedly became engineer and manager of Fernando Castro's sawmill on the Osa Peninsula near Golfo Dulce. The attaché treated the report as further evidence of Japanese interest in a strategically located Pacific harbor.

subfiles.title: Report No. 4,388: La Tribuna and pro-Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Alex A. Cohen, in charge of the Military Attaché's office
subfiles.to: U.S. military intelligence and State Department channels
subfiles.about: Assesses La Tribuna as the principal outlet for Japanese propaganda in San José.
subfiles.summary: The report says La Tribuna had increasingly become a standard-bearer for Japanese propaganda. It links the newspaper to former foreign secretary Manuel Francisco Jiménez and editor José María Pinaud, while suggesting that opponents of President Cortés may have used pro-Japanese coverage to embarrass his administration with the United States.

subfiles.title: File note on possible Japanese purchase of the Pacific Refrigeration Company
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Cross-references Despatch No. 312 on Japanese interest in purchasing a Puntarenas refrigeration plant.
subfiles.summary: The note concerns a possible sale of the Pacific Refrigeration Company to Japanese interests. It records that Japanese operators off Puntarenas had approached the company and later tried to arrange a meeting with its manager in San José.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 312: Financial difficulties of the Pacific Refrigeration Company
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, American Minister at San José
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese interests sought to acquire a financially troubled American-operated tuna plant.
subfiles.summary: General Manager John G. Robertson told Hornibrook that equipment failure had spoiled about 240 tons of tuna and that the company needed roughly $5,000 to continue operating. Japanese interests at Puntarenas had repeatedly approached Robertson about acquiring the plant, but he regarded a sale to Mr. Amano as a last resort. Robertson instead planned to seek a Costa Rican bank loan or government relief.

subfiles.title: File note on Robertson's loan application
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Reports a pending Banco de Costa Rica decision on financing the Pacific Refrigeration Company.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references Telegram No. 40 concerning possible Japanese acquisition of the company. Robertson's loan application was to be considered by the bank's directors on July 10, and approval remained possible.

subfiles.title: File note on Banco de Costa Rica's initial loan refusal
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Reports the bank's initial refusal to finance the Pacific Refrigeration Company.
subfiles.summary: The Banco de Costa Rica declined the loan because the company's account had been maintained at a rival bank. The note adds that the question would be reopened and that the loan might still be granted.

subfiles.title: File note for Despatch No. 334
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, U.S. Legation at San José
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch on the refrigeration company's finances and fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Despatch No. 334 as a report on Japanese activities in Costa Rica. It specifically mentions the financial difficulties of the Pacific Refrigeration Company and the activities of fishing boats.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 334: Financial difficulties of the Pacific Refrigeration Company
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, American Minister at San José
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum on Robertson's financial negotiations and the bank's position.
subfiles.summary: Hornibrook reports that Secretary Robert Y. Brown discussed the company's finances with John G. Robertson during a visit to Puntarenas. The Banco de Costa Rica had initially rejected the loan because the company banked with a competitor, but an American bank officer indicated that discussions could be reopened when Robertson returned to San José.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Pacific Refrigeration Company's financial position
subfiles.from: Robert Y. Brown
subfiles.about: Explains Robertson's negotiations with officials, banks, fishing vessels and a U.S. seafood purchaser.
subfiles.summary: Brown reports that Francisco Pacheco was sympathetic but offered no concrete aid, while Claudio Cortés and the Pacific Railway might provide limited relief. Fishermen agreed to share losses from spoiled shipments and accept reimbursement in ice, with the Japanese-owned Amano proving more accommodating than expected. The Van Camp Seafood Company authorized $3,000 in advances, leaving Robertson cautiously confident that operations could continue.

subfiles.title: Report on charitable donations by Japanese residents
subfiles.from: Alex A. Cohen, in charge of the Military Attaché's office
subfiles.about: Treats a donation by Kenko Kawakubo and Sanoko Megurikani as Japanese public-relations activity.
subfiles.summary: Diario de Costa Rica reported that the two women donated $100 to La Casa de la Madre y del Niño, headed by Julia Fernández de Cortés. The report reproduces their laudatory letter and interprets the conspicuous gift as an effort to ingratiate Japanese residents with Costa Rican society and the president's family.

subfiles.title: File note on suspension of the Pacific Refrigeration Company
subfiles.from: Navy Department
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on the suspension of Pacific Refrigeration Company activities.
subfiles.summary: The note says Yoshitaro Amano, owner of the vessel Amano, reported that the Pacific Refrigeration Company had suspended operations. Activities were expected to remain halted until December 25.

subfiles.title: Colonel Montúfar's letter warning of Japanese activity
subfiles.from: Colonel Gerard F. Montúfar
subfiles.about: Warns the President about Japanese economic and strategic activity in Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: Although the surviving OCR is badly degraded, the letter discusses Costa Rican commerce, Japanese activity and implications for the United States and the Panama Canal. Montúfar appears to portray Japanese commercial and agricultural preparations as a source of strategic danger and urges U.S. attention. He signs as Colonel Gerard F. Montúfar and gives a San José postal address.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 166: No reply to Colonel Montúfar
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs that no reply be made to Colonel Montúfar's letter.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to the Legation's despatch explaining why acknowledgment of Montúfar's communication would be undesirable. It accepts that reasoning and states that no reply to Colonel Montúfar is necessary.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 159 transmitting proposed reply to Colonel Montúfar
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a proposed letter to Montúfar and a copy of his communication to the President.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends the Legation a letter addressed to Colonel Gerard F. Montúfar for delivery if the minister perceives no objection. A copy of Montúfar's November 28 letter to the President is enclosed for the Legation's information.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 528: Proposed acknowledgment of Colonel Montúfar's letter
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, American Minister at San José
subfiles.about: Recommends against acknowledging Montúfar's letter because of his lack of standing and hostility toward the government.
subfiles.summary: Hornibrook explains that Gerard F. Montúfar was an honorary colonel with no official position and was estranged from his brother, Foreign Minister Zúñiga Montúfar, and from the Cortés administration. He recounts Montúfar's drunken fight at the Italian Legation and his attacks on the president and foreign minister over the Panama–Costa Rica boundary. Hornibrook warns that Montúfar would exploit any acknowledgment as official recognition.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to East Pacific Fishery Company report
subfiles.from: Military Attaché, Costa Rica (J. B. Pate)
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Yoshitaro Amano's East Pacific Fishery Company.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Report No. 4,650 as concerning Japanese fishing activities in Costa Rica. It states that Yoshitaro Amano organized a Costa Rican company called the East Pacific Fishery Company.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on two Amano fishing boats
subfiles.from: U.S. Naval Attaché
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Department of State channels
subfiles.about: Forwards photographs of two fishing boats owned by Yoshitaro Amano.
subfiles.summary: The report transmits two photographs supplied by the secretary of the Military Attaché in San José. Both vessels were owned by Yoshitaro Amano and operated from Puntarenas; the OCR does not preserve their names reliably.

subfiles.title: Confidential-file filing sheet
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Records that the associated material was placed in the confidential file.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the decimal-file number and a filing notation. It confirms that the preceding material was retained in the Department's confidential file.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs summary of Despatch No. 1504 from Panama
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.to: Internal State, War and Navy Department readers
subfiles.about: Summarizes allegations of espionage and drug trafficking within the Japanese colony in Panama.
subfiles.summary: The summary states that an April 26 despatch from the American Legation in Panama transmitted clippings and an attorney's memorandum alleging numerous unregistered Japanese residents. Many allegedly had unexplained means of support and were suspected of espionage or narcotics trafficking. The division judged the material potentially useful to the War and Navy Departments.
